name: Umar Kowalski

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the office administrator at a small architecture practice, fourteen people above a bakery on the high street of a county town. I do the diaries, the site visit bookings, the planning application paperwork, timesheets and invoices, and I keep the drawing archive from falling apart. I use AI every day, for summarising council emails and tidying up meeting notes, and I've set up a few little automations that file things for me.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like fixing broken processes, like when I cut the timesheet chase from two days to twenty minutes with a form and a reminder bot. What wears me out is the money: lower pay than in the city, and I share a flat with two mates and still have barely a fortnight saved. There aren't many office jobs in this town, so I can't just walk out if I get fed up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. I'll read it out. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it was always going to be a useful tool rather than magic. I'd probably post that the hype mostly made a few companies rich. At work I'd keep showing people the small time-savers that actually work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's mostly fine, because I already use the useful bits. The worry is money, not AI. If the practice has a slow year, like when the housing scheme fell through last spring, the first thing they freeze is pay rises for people like me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep building small automations for the office and write down how much time each one saves. Then I'd take that list to the partners at my review and ask for a proper pay rise. I'd also try to put a hundred a month into savings, because a fortnight's cushion is silly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, more about money than machines. I feel fine about the work and tight about the rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the partners actually pay you more for saving time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe not straight away. Rachel (one of the two partners) once told me admin is a cost, not an investment. But if I can show her I saved twelve hours a month, that's a number, and architects like numbers on drawings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would happen if they said no?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd look further afield, probably the city, which means a ninety-minute train each way. Or I'd ask about doing some project coordination work alongside admin. I'd rather grow where I am than commute, honestly.

say: I'd say AI was always a **useful tool**, not magic.
I'd post that the **hype** mostly made a few companies rich.
think: I already use the **useful bits**, so the work feels fine.
My worry is **money**: a slow year means pay freezes for admin.
do: Keep building **small automations** and log the hours saved.
Take that list to my **pay review**.
Save **a hundred a month** to grow a fortnight's cushion.
feel: **Uneasy**, fine about the work but tight about the rent.
S0.quote: I feel fine about the work and tight about the rent.
fieldNote: Umar is already a **daily AI user**, so the mild picture changes little for him.
His real pressure is **low pay** and a thin cushion in a town with few office jobs.
He plans to turn **time saved** into an argument for a raise.

steps.text: Build more office automations and log the hours each saves
Take the hours-saved list to his pay review with the partners
Put a hundred a month into savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. I'll read it out. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is where we need to be loud about sharing the gains. If software does half the admin in every office, the hours saved should mean shorter weeks or better pay, not just bigger profits. I'd be saying that on every forum I'm on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'm one of the people who comes out all right, as long as I move fast. The booking, invoicing and planning paperwork all go to software. Somebody still has to set it up and fix it when it breaks, and in a fourteen-person practice that's whoever already knows how, which is me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to the partners in the first month with a plan to set up the new systems myself, and ask for a new title, something like operations coordinator, with a raise. I'd take an evening course in project coordination. And I'd join the tech workers' union, because even people who do all right need someone pushing for the rest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but excited, if that's allowed. I like this kind of problem.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you come out all right. What if the partners just buy a package that needs no one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'm out, and that's a real risk. The software companies do sell it as needing no one. But in my experience nothing in a small office works without someone poking the software daily, and I'd bet a month's wages on that if I had one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who in the office would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Jun (the part-time bookkeeper), who's in her fifties and does the accounts on paper first and then types them in. The accounts software would do most of her job. I'd try to teach her, but she'd have to want it.

say: I'd say the hours saved should mean **shorter weeks** or **better pay**.
I'd argue for **sharing the gains** on every forum I'm on.
think: Booking, invoicing and **planning paperwork** all go to software.
Somebody has to **set up and fix** it, and that's probably me.
do: Pitch the partners in the **first month** to run the new systems.
Ask for an **operations coordinator** title with a raise.
Join the **tech workers' union** and take a project coordination course.
feel: **Uneasy** but excited, because he likes this kind of problem.
S1.quote: Nothing in a small office works without someone poking the software daily, and I'd bet a month's wages on that if I had one.
fieldNote: Umar expects to **keep his job** by becoming the one who runs the systems.
He admits the risk of a **no-staff package** but bets against it.
He is adaptive yet still **progressive**: he joins a union and worries for Jun.

steps.text: Set up the practice's new booking and invoice software himself
Learn the new practice software inside out in the first month
Take an evening course in project coordination

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. I'll read it out. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment for a basic income and public ownership of some of this stuff, because two years is a cliff, not a change. I'd be at the protests and in the group chats organising them. At work I'd say we need to talk about it as a team, today.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years scares me even though I'm the one who likes this stuff. If AI can do any thinking work, it can also set itself up and fix itself, so my clever plan from the slow version doesn't last. And architects themselves get squeezed, so the practice might shrink to the two partners and a computer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the two years to get into something with my hands that robots don't reach until 2031, maybe site work with the builders we work with, as an assistant site manager. I'd ask our main contractor about it straight away. I'd also cut spending hard and move to a cheaper room, to build three months of savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. It's the first time this stuff has made me feel stupid for liking it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you actually move to site work, from an office?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I've been on site visits loads, and I like it more than I let on. Tony (the site manager at our main contractor) said I'd be good at it because I'm organised. It's mud and early starts, but it's three more years of work, and those three years matter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your flatmates?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to get their CVs together and stop assuming somebody's got a plan. One of them works in a call centre, so he's even more exposed than me. We'd probably talk about moving somewhere cheaper together.

say: I'd call for **basic income** and some **public ownership**.
I'd organise **protests** and push my team to talk today.
think: If AI can **fix itself**, my plan to run the systems fails.
The practice might shrink to **two partners** and a computer.
do: Ask our main contractor about **assistant site manager** work straight away.
Move to a **cheaper room** and cut spending hard.
Build **three months** of savings over the two years.
feel: **Alarmed**, and for the first time foolish for liking this technology.
S2.quote: Two years scares me even though I'm the one who likes this stuff.
fieldNote: Even adaptive Umar sees his **systems plan** fail when AI can maintain itself.
He grabs the **three-year gap** before robots by moving towards site work.
Thin savings push him to **move cheaper** and build a cushion fast.

steps.text: Ask the main contractor's site manager about assistant site manager work
Move into a cheaper room with his flatmates
Cut spending to build three months of savings
Help organise protests through his group chats

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called AGI by 2031. I'll read it out. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years, so let's not waste them arguing whether it's real. I'd push for retraining funds and for unions to be in the room with the big firms. And I'd keep telling people to use the tools so they understand what's coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is enough for me to make a proper move. I'd still be the systems person for a couple of years, and that buys me a pay rise and some savings. Then I'd shift to site management or something hands-on before 2031, so I land just as the office work goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the operations coordinator role first and save hard from the raise. In year two I'd start the part-time construction site management certificate. I'd keep my AI skills sharp because site managers will use it too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a way that makes me want to get going. I'd sleep okay most nights.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why anxious and not calm, if you have a plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the plan needs things to go right, and I've got barely a fortnight saved. One bad year at the practice and the raise doesn't happen. And robots on site still arrive in 2034, so I'm moving towards a door that also closes, just later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gets cut first if the raise doesn't come?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The gym and the weekend trips back to my parents, which costs about eighty a month in train fares. I'd still pay the course fees, because those are the way out.

say: I'd say we have **five years**, so stop arguing about whether it's real.
I'd push for **retraining funds** and **unions** in the room.
think: Being the **systems person** for two years buys a raise and savings.
Then I'd move to **site management** before 2031.
do: Take the **operations coordinator** role and save the raise.
Start the **site management certificate** in year two.
Keep **AI skills** sharp for site work.
feel: **Anxious**, but in a way that makes me want to get going.
S3.quote: Robots on site still arrive in 2034, so I'm moving towards a door that also closes, just later.
fieldNote: Umar builds a **two-step plan**: systems role first, then site management.
He stays **anxious** because the plan depends on a raise and he has a fortnight saved.
He sees site work as a **later door**, not a safe one.

steps.text: Take the operations coordinator role and bank the raise
Start the part-time site management certificate in year two
Keep using AI tools daily to stay sharp
Drop the gym and the monthly train trips home

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. I'll read it out. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years means there's no excuse for anyone to be caught out. Governments should be building retraining and income support now. I'd also say it's a chance to make work shorter for everyone, if we organise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is honestly fine for me. I'm twenty-seven, so I'd be thirty-seven, with time to become a site manager or move into something like building surveying. My worry would be more about other people, and whether the town still has jobs at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the operations role, then the site management certificate, then maybe a surveying qualification part-time. I'd save steadily, aiming for six months by thirty. I'd stay active in the union because a decade is a long time to build something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, mostly for the town. For me it feels like a decent puzzle with time on the clock.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you mean about the town?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Half the high street is offices like ours: estate agents, solicitors, insurance. If AGI takes those, the bakery under us loses its lunch trade. I might be fine, but I don't want to be fine in a dead town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move away?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, if work dried up. But my parents are here and I like it. I'd rather help build something here, maybe a co-op of trades people, than leave.

say: I'd say ten years leaves **no excuse** for anyone to be caught out.
I'd push to make work **shorter for everyone**.
think: At **thirty-seven** I could be a site manager or surveyor.
My worry is whether the **town** still has jobs.
do: Do the **operations role**, then site management, then surveying.
Save steadily towards **six months** by thirty.
Stay active in the **union** over the decade.
feel: **Uneasy** for the town, but it feels like a puzzle with time.
S4.quote: I might be fine, but I don't want to be fine in a dead town.
fieldNote: With ten years Umar feels **personally safe** enough; his worry shifts to the high street.
He imagines a **trades co-op**, mixing progressive views with practical plans.
He wants to **stay** near his parents rather than move.

steps.text: Move from operations coordinator to a site management certificate
Save steadily towards six months of expenses by thirty

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because even my best plan stops working when the AI can fix itself. What would help is a basic income floor while people move, and paid apprenticeships for adults in site and trade work, not just for teenagers.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask who's actually choosing which jobs go. It's not the people in the office, it's the people selling the software and the partners buying it. I spend all day making machines save time, and I've never once been asked what the time should be used for.

headlineQuote: I spend all day making machines save time, and I've never once been asked what the time should be used for.
portrait: Umar is **27**, office administrator at a small architecture practice in a county town, sharing a flat with two friends.
He uses AI **every day** and builds small automations, but has barely a **fortnight** saved.
He's **progressive**: wants gains shared, joins a union, and worries for older colleagues.
In slower pictures he plans a **systems role**, then a move into site management.
He's alarmed at two years, but only **uneasy** at ten, worrying more for the town.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because AI that fixes itself ends his systems plan.
whatWouldHelp: A **basic income** floor while people move between jobs.
Paid **adult apprenticeships** in site and trade work.
